Renault Forefront Is a Cabinless Remote-Controlled Robotic Truck Meant for the Military
6 photos
Photo: Renault
Historically speaking, especially in times of need, carmakers have always been involved in the defense industry. Because the times we now live in are a tad quieter than they used to be (yes, despite the wars raging in Ukraine, Iran, and elsewhere), we don't see carmakers, especially the European ones, as involved as they used to be with the military. That's why an announcement made by French carmaker Renault earlier this month came a bit as a surprise.
For no apparent reason, Renault announced at the beginning of this month a tie-up with Belgian defense contractor and mechanical engineering firm John Cockerill for the creation of something called the Forefront concept.
A cabinless wheeled platform by trade, the Forefront is meant, for now, as a remotely operated ground platform targeted first and foremost at the defense industry, where it could be used for a variety of purposes, including logistics support, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR), anti-drone operations, fire support and evacuation.
The platform has been designed by the two companies with input from the French armed forces as a tool to conduct remote operations in high-risk areas. Not all its details are known, but the French did share enough about it for us to form a pretty decent idea of what to expect.
Powered by two electric motors of undisclosed capabilities, the design is four-wheel drive, with all four wheels steerable, which makes it capable of tackling pretty much all sorts of terrain imaginable.
There is probably a battery pack on deck as well, completed by a confirmed range extender, but we only know that it is enough to ensure a maximum range of some 249 miles (400 km). All of that, of course, traveled in a silent fashion.
The design is modular, meaning it can accommodate a wide range of payloads, as long as their combined weight doesn't exceed one ton. This approach also makes it capable of being rapidly industrialized at a relatively low cost.
For the Forefront, Renault was responsible for the design of the platform, while John Cockerill was responsible for the remote-operation system, the autonomy functions that it the near future could make it capable of doing things all on its own, mission-system integration and operational support.
The design is presently still in the concept stage, but the parties responsible for it said that it will be tested in the real world soon. Several exercises and trials are planned in the coming weeks, but no details on what that means have been provided.
If it proves its worth (we'll keep an eye on it and report back once we know more about that), the Forefront could also be considered for use for civilian purposes, including civil protection operations, logistics, and missions in constrained or hazardous working environments.

Second Owner Ditching His 1969 Pontiac GTO: Original 242, So Many Secrets
21 photos
Photo: Facebook Marketplace
I wouldn’t blame anyone for being fascinated by this orange GTO. I was, too, as the car looks delicious, to say the least. This 1969 GTO is looking for a new home, with the seller revealing that it is already running great.
This means that you should be able to jump behind the wheel the moment you pay the price, but here’s the obligatory recommendation.
You’d better call the seller and ask all your questions because the closer you get, the more the all-original dream fades away. This car is no longer original, but that shouldn’t be a problem if you know precisely what to expect. That’s why I recommend that an in-person inspection is recommended, though if you can’t do this, a video call and a walkaround video should also come in handy.
Photo: Facebook Marketplace We all already know what the 1969 model year represented for the Pontiac GTO . With insurance companies no longer being big fans of muscle cars, the GTO took a hit and dropped to 72,287 units. It was still a great model year for the GTO, and the debut of the Judge is probably the most notable thing that happened in 1969.
The Judge is now the most desirable, the most valuable, the most you name it version of the Pontiac GTO today. It’s a configuration that collectors are willing to pay big bucks for, especially when these cars check the right boxes and are still original and fitted with the right goodies.
Non-Judge GTOs are lovable, too. Pontiac continued to offer a de-tuned version of the base engine, once again with 265 horsepower, but fortunately, few buyers ended up going back when ordering a GTO. This didn’t make any sense anyway, so most buyers decided to stick with the base configuration or pay extra for upgraded power.
The 366-horsepower upgrade to the Ram Air III configuration could be had for only $342, and needless to say, many people took advantage of this offer. A Ram Air IV setup was also available, developing 370 horsepower on the Judge.
Photo: Facebook Marketplace While it is a true GTO, and the 242 code in the VIN confirms this, our specimen no longer has the original engine under the hood.
The owner points to a 428 code YH unit with 360 horsepower.
A 428 was not available on the GTO in 1969, as all engines a Goat buyer could install on the car this year were variations of the 400.
On the other hand, 428 engines were offered on Pontiac’s big cars, including the Catalina and the Bonneville. The YH code represents the standard 428 four-barrel engine that was typically paired with a TH400 transmission. It produced 360 horsepower, just like the owner advertises in their Facebook post.
So no, this GTO no longer has the original engine under the hood, but it is now fitted with a larger unit donated by another Pontiac. No other information was shared about this engine swap, but considering the car is only at its second owner, figuring out what happened shouldn’t be that hard.
Photo: Facebook Marketplace Another thing that is no longer original is the paint. While the orange paint looks great and makes me think of Hugger Orange (sorry, Pontiac fans), this isn’t the original color that this GTO shipped with. The vehicle was originally gray, and the owner explains that the color was changed at some point in the car’s life.
The seller briefly mentions a previous restoration, and there’s a chance this was the moment when the new engine was installed and the gray paint was replaced with orange. Another part that was likely updated as part of this process is the interior, which has also received a complete refresh, also getting the changes that you see in the photos.
The original dash was no longer working, so new gauges were installed. This is a no-AC car but has disc brakes on all four wheels.
Photo: Facebook Marketplace As anyone would expect, a Pontiac GTO is still a Pontiac GTO, so this car can’t sell for beer money. This makes perfect sense, considering the 1969 model year is one of the most desirable in the history of the GTO, so it’ll be interesting to see how fast this specimen finds a new home.
Convincing someone to pay the right price for a GTO that was so heavily altered isn’t necessarily easy, but Pontiac has lots of fans across the US, so it’ll sell eventually.
The owner believes $39,000 is a fair price for this car, and I don’t think they are very far from the actual price of the car. I still recommend that you call them and request additional information, and if you want to make sure that what you see is what you get, you’ll have to pay the man a visit at his garage in Chula Vista, California.
Considering the car’s shape, you should be able to drive it back on its wheels.

After emraclidine’s schizophrenia fail and Cobenfy’s laggard launch, it’s too early to know who made the better buy: AbbVie, in its $8.7 billion Cerevel takeover in late 2023, or Bristol Myers Squibb, which spent $14 billion for Karuna just two weeks later.
Earlier this fall, the FDA approved AbbVie’s Parkinson’s disease drug Juvmo—formerly tavapadon — prompting analysts and observers to revisit the pharma’s $8.7 billion takeover of Cerevel Therapeutics, along with a parallel transaction: Bristol Myers Squibb’s $14 billion buyout of Karuna Therapeutics. But at least one analyst says it’s too early for a reckoning on either transaction.
“It’s still early days, but as of today, I don’t think there’s a clear winner,” Graig Suvannavejh, managing director and senior biotech and biopharma analyst at Mizuho Securities, told BioSpace .
Less than a year after AbbVie bought Cerevel in December 2023, the centerpiece of the buyout, schizophrenia drug emraclidine, failed two Phase 2 studies . The news sent the pharma’s shares crashing 12% and led analysts to question its decision to move on Cerevel. The failure looked even worse given that competing schizophrenia candidate KarXT, which BMS picked up in its acquisition of Karuna Therapeutics just two weeks after AbbVie’s Cerevel play, had just won the FDA’s blessing and entered the market as Cobenfy, the first novel schizophrenia drug in more than three decades.
But with Juvmo’s approval, and Cobenfy struggling to meet sales expectations, the ultimate value of both deals is looking less clear cut.
Matt Phipps, group head of biotechnology equity research at William Blair, agreed that AbbVie’s buy is not down for the count yet. “At the time of the Cerevel acquisition no one was really thinking about tavapadon,” he told BioSpace in an email. Its September approval “clearly should offer some support” for the deal, he added.
Meanwhile, Cobenfy has long disappointed. After exceeding expectations in the fourth quarter of 2024, its first full quarter on the market, the drug began to slip. In 2025, Cobenfy brought in $155 million in sales , less than half of some analysts’ initial predictions, Suvannavejh previously told BioSpace , and sales continued to miss expectations in 2026.
“I’m not sure anyone would declare victory there,” Suvannavejh said of Cobenfy’s sales to date. “You certainly don’t want to pay $14 billion to get that kind of sales trajectory.”
As for AbbVie’s Cerevel buy, he added, the pharma gained a pipeline beyond emraclidine—and it is still working on that asset as well.
Schizophrenia
FDA Approves First Novel Schizophrenia Drug in 35 Years
BMS’ KarXT targets muscarinic receptors and “is at least 2-3 years ahead of the competition” including AbbVie and Neurocrine Biosciences, Truist Securities wrote in a note to investors.
September 27, 2024
·
8 min read
·
Heather McKenzie
Read more
Cobenfy’s tolerability troubles
In addition to the timing, the size of the deals and the neuro focus of both, the AbbVie and BMS deals are often put in the same bucket because the schizophrenia assets that starred in those transactions both act on the muscarinic receptors. It’s difficult to pinpoint where Cobenfy went wrong, but Suvannavejh flagged its safety profile as one issue.
“I think that is part of the reason why Cobenfy commercially has not done that well because . . . the side effects, the GI adverse events, are likely to be in the real world much worse than what was reported in the Phase 3 studies.”
MapLight CEO Christopher Kroeger agreed .
“The challenge with Cobenfy has been that it is not proven to be particularly tolerable,” Kroeger told BioSpace in August. Because Cobenfy’s components—the muscarinic agonist xanomeline and the muscarinic antagonist trospium chloride—have to be in exquisite balance, there can be high interpatient variability, he added.
Even as Cobenfy’s market uptake continues to be a challenge, BMS is pushing the drug forward in Alzheimer’s disease psychosis, positioning it as a safer option versus current antipsychotics on the market, most of which have boxed warnings for an elevated risk of death in older patients with dementia.
But readouts from the ADEPT program studying Cobenfy in this indication keep being pushed back, impeded by enrollment problems and the slow accrual of outcome events. BMS had originally expected data from the ADEPT-2 trial by the end of last year, but announced in December 2025 that the results would instead come by the end of this year. In July, BMS disclosed another delay for the program, with CEO Chris Boerner saying on the company’s second quarter earnings call that topline data readouts from ADEPT are now anticipated in early 2027, with a potential interim analysis for ADEPT-1 later this year.
Earnings
BMS positions Cobenfy as safer alternative ahead of pivotal Alzheimer’s psychosis readout
After delaying a late-stage readout last year due to “irregularities” at certain study sites, pivotal data for Bristol Myers Squibb’s Cobenfy appear set to arrive later this year.
April 30, 2026
·
2 min read
·
Tristan Manalac
Read more
While delays to readouts don’t necessarily mean that those studies failed, Suvannavejh indicated it’s not something analysts regard positively.
BMS is also studying Cobenfy in bipolar mania, Alzheimer’s disease agitation, Alzheimer’s disease cognition and pediatric autism irritability.
Cerevel: A riskier bet
Cobenfy may be struggling on the market, but for Suvannavejh, AbbVie’s Cerevel acquisition was always the riskier of the two bets.
In December 2023, when both deals went down, Karuna was farther along in the drug development journey. Cobenfy, still known as KarXT at the time, already had two Phase 3 studies under its belt, both of which had demonstrated the drug’s benefits. Meanwhile, Cerevel’s emraclidine had only cleared Phase 1b testing and was still wrapping up two registration-enabling Phase 2 studies. This is possibly what enabled Karuna to be sold at a higher valuation, Suvannavejh explained.
“AbbVie, I guess, jumped the gun and said, ‘Well, we have a lot of confidence that the Phase 2/3 data will be positive,’” he continued. While the earlier-stage asset may have saved AbbVie a few billion dollars, the pharma gambled by “buying something that’s less derisked.”
But the book isn’t closed on emraclidine just yet. AbbVie is studying the molecule in a Phase 2 trial in adults with schizophrenia. The asset is also in early-stage development for psychosis, with data for both indications slated for this year .
Of the Juvmo approval, Suvannavejh said it’s difficult to predict peak sales, and noted that a lot of Parkinson’s drugs, which are mostly symptomatic treatments, “don’t tend to be blockbuster products.”
William Blair projects Juvmo to make $1.4 billion in 2040. Even assuming the drug’s peak sales were to reach four to five times the firm’s estimate, Phipps is unconvinced it will justify AbbVie’s Cerevel buy.
“You probably aren’t fully justifying the take out price of Cerevel,” he told BioSpace . “So I think many people would say they overpaid, but at least were fortunate to have it not be a complete zero.”
Editor’s note: Heather McKenzie contributed reporting to this piece.

This Application Turns Your Outdated Tablet Into a New-Gen Android Auto-Like Head Unit
6 photos
Photo: Aurora Dash developer
While the number of car launchers on the Google Play Store is, well, significant, finding an application that works on an ancient Android version is quite a challenge. That’s why Aurora Dash caught my attention.
Here’s the thing. If you run Android 17 on the tablet or Android-powered head unit in your car and think that everybody else is doing the same, you are so wrong. Many Android units run an outdated version of the operating system for a very simple reason: they come from generic Chinese brands that offer zero software support, so the OS version they shipped with is still the one they run today.
In other words, there are lots of tablets and head units out there running an old version of Android. For their owners, these devices are almost of no use.
Aurora Dash changes this, as it even supports Android 10. “Many head units say Android 13 or 14 but run something older underneath,” the developer explains.
If you checked the main photo in this article, there’s a good chance you thought this was Android Auto. I wouldn’t blame anyone for thinking the same, and while this interface looks inspired by Android Auto, it pushes the Coolwalk-based UI a step further.
Photo: Aurora Dash developer The left side of the screen is still being used by the navigation app - in this case, Google Maps - while the remaining space on the screen goes to various applications that show data in panels, more like widgets, similar to those on the Coolwalk screen on Android Auto. You get a media player, a clock, a weather widget, and a speedometer, all shown on the same screen at the same time.
So why should you install Aurora Dash and not another car launcher from the Google Play Store if the Android version is not an issue in your case?
The developer has created a “what makes it different” section that speaks for itself. You get an ad-free OEM-like interface that uses the entire screen estate, a dock that floats over any app (so if you’re also using other apps on your Android device, you’ll also get access to home, back, and other buttons), and left- and right-hand drive layouts.
Photo: Aurora Dash developer The application can adapt to your screen aspect ratio, so if you have a portrait-based Android head unit, you’ll still see the right interface. The developer touts standard, ultra-wide (such as the ones in some BMW models) and vertical units with 12- or 14-inch displays.
The application is currently in beta, waiting for Google Play Store approval, and before you head over to the comments section to express your vibe-coding thoughts, the developer is committed to releasing frequent updates. The most recent version fixes a series of bugs and adds new clock faces, a compass, new weather icons, and bigger music buttons on large high-res screens.
While the UI might look familiar for those who have used Android Auto before, especially thanks to the tile-based interface, I do think that some of these tiles aren’t necessarily useful and only use valuable estate on a screen that should be as uncluttered as possible.
Photo: Aurora Dash developer For example, a dedicated speedometer tile doesn’t make much sense, considering Google Maps already shows the current speed directly on the main screen. The same for the clock, which already appears in the status bar on the Android device. While it’s larger and easier to read, the clock tile uses too much space, and many drivers might prefer to see a larger Google Maps title rather than redundant data.
Future updates should include more customization options and let drivers decide what tiles to display on the screen, especially if they want the navigation app to show more data. The dev already allows users to choose what navigation app they want to run on the screen, with Google Maps and Waze obviously supported. Other names like Sygic, OsmAnd, and Magic Earth can also be used with Aurora Dash.
Light and dark modes are also available, and the application sports several welcome extras, such as weather warnings if you drive in the United States, Canada, or Norway, and album art for the media player.
Photo: Aurora Dash developer Another big benefit of this app is that it’s extremely lightweight. The app’s size is only 3 MB, so it can be installed even on those units with very limited storage space. It should also start fast and work smoothly, though I’ll only be able to tell this for sure after I try out the application.
The developer says the application should run on any Android head unit powered by at least Android 10, CarPlay and Android Auto AI boxes that run Android, Android tablets installed in a car, and units without system buttons (thanks to the dock that remains on the screen all the time). If your infotainment screen can’t install apps and is built for Android Auto, it won’t be able to run this launcher.

Inclusion of the patient perspective is currently an “optional” part of the rare disease drug development process, CBER Director Karim Mikhail told BioSpace . Mikhail, along with his CDER counterpart Michael Davis and other agency rare disease leaders, is trying to change that.
The voices of patients with a rare disease are sometimes heard by the FDA—at listening sessions and during advisory committee meetings—but for biologics head Karim Mikhail, it isn’t enough.
These opportunities currently come late in the drug development cycle, as therapies are on the cusp of potential market entry. “We need to have sponsors, experts and patients engaged in the process from early on,” Mikhail, director of the Center for Biologics Research and Evaluation (CBER), told BioSpace in an interview—right from the time companies seek permission to test their assets in humans.
Only then can substantive changes be implemented based on patient feedback. Today, when patients are heard during adcomm meetings, “that’s way too late,” Mikhail said. “The clinical development is already defined. Everything is already set.”
Under the FDA’s new Rare Disease Framework Initiative , unveiled last month, drug sponsors should expect that the patient perspective will be an essential component of the regulatory submission, Mikhail said. Patient input will be used to define several elements of a rare disease development program, he continued, from a clinical endpoint that is “actually meaningful” to an understanding of the benefit-risk ratio. This is a question that should be answered by those who are afflicted, he said, not people who don’t have the disease.
FDA
FDA’s latest rare disease framework seeks to prioritize consistency in flexibility
Following several recent initiatives, the FDA’s newest rare disease framework sets out to standardize the agency’s approach to scientific evidence and bring rare disease therapies to patients faster.
October 15, 2026
·
4 min read
·
Michael Gibney
Read more
Sponsors will need to come to these early meetings prepared to discuss issues like endpoint selection, based on what’s important to patients, Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) director Michael Davis told BioSpace in the same interview. Drug developers will also need to define the trial methodology—including number of trials—along with the control group and analysis plan.
This renewed emphasis on the patient voice in rare disease drug development should be music to the ears of many—including patients.
A public meeting held by the FDA on Oct. 28 to solicit feedback on the new framework has already garnered 63 comments. One anonymous writer implored the agency to “give patients and families a formal voice on acceptable risk. People living with a rare, progressive disease are entitled to weigh risks that a regulator might not choose for them.”
The FDA’s journey to incorporate patients
As with many facets of the FDA’s new rare disease framework, inclusion of the patient voice is not a novel concept.
Patient-focused drug development began in earnest across the agency nearly 15 years ago, with the fifth reauthorization of the Prescription Drug User Fee Act (PDUFA V) in 2012. In that legislation, the FDA committed to evolving the benefit-risk framework, Robyn Bent, director of CDER’s Patient Focused Drug Development Program, told BioSpace on the sidelines of the BIO 2026 conference in June.
“We, of course, also agreed that it’s really hard to understand that therapeutic context without hearing from patients,” Bent said. So the FDA set out to hold 24 condition-specific, patient-focused drug development meetings, where patients with rare diseases could share their experiences.
When these meetings began, Bent continued, “we started hearing that, basically, the patient perspective wasn’t really being incorporated. The endpoints that were being measured weren’t endpoints that mattered to patients [and] clinical trial participation excluded too many people.”
Since then, the FDA has seen an increase in sponsors incorporating the patient voice, she added. “A lot of industry has been very responsive and has worked to incorporate the patient perspective.”
Bent has seen patient experience data included in meeting requests and packages and regulatory applications. That said, “obviously there’s more room to go,” she added.
“Patient experience data has a different kind of importance when you’re talking about diseases that are not super well characterized.”
Innovative trial design
One of the most contentious questions in rare disease drug development has been the use of external controls in clinical trials. Externally controlled studies—those using historical or real-world data—have contributed to recent FDA rejections, including of REGENXBIO’s Hunter syndrome gene therapy , and reversals of regulatory guidance, such as for uniQure’s gene therapy for Huntington’s disease .
FDA
FDA Reversals in Rare Disease Space Highlight Confusion Around External Controls
While recent FDA guidance speaks to the agency’s support of innovative trial designs—including the use of external controls—the application of this flexibility appears to be inconsistent. One former regulator says the situation is more nuanced.
April 6, 2026
·
6 min read
·
Heather McKenzie
Read more
Yet agency guidance has supported the use of these innovative trial designs. This includes 2023 draft guidance focused solely on the use of external controls. More recently, in September 2025, the FDA published draft guidance for cell and gene therapy trial design that includes externally controlled studies as one option, as well as the novel Rare Disease Evidence Principles (RDEP) program, focused on therapies for ultrarare diseases. Under the RDEP, treatments for diseases affecting very small patient populations—typically less than 1,000 individuals—may only need to provide evidence from a single-arm trial, in addition to “ strong confirmatory evidence ,” including from case reports and expanded access data, such as natural history .
The FDA’s new framework echoes this sentiment, championing “the use of cutting-edge science, novel methods and clinical trial designs, and innovative statistical approaches in the development of rare disease therapies,” though it stops short of specifically addressing the use of external controls.
Nasha Fitter, co-founder of the FOXG1 Research Foundation and mom of Amara, who has a rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorder called FOXG1 syndrome, implored the FDA to specifically address the use of external controls. She explained that her “clinical advisors pushed back” on a newly curated database of medical records for use in the foundation’s single open-label trial of an investigational gene therapy for the disease.
Natural history data for FOXG1 was “nonexistent,” Fitter explained in a statement following an Oct. 28 public meeting held by the agency to discuss the new framework. This spurred her foundation to create a database from the medical records of more than 100 children with the disease. These data then shaped the foundation’s endpoints and became the external control for the trial. But because the FDA hasn’t clearly stated its position on external controls, the foundation’s advisors balked at their plan, Fitter explained in her statement, which she shared with BioSpace in an email. “There was no regulatory guidance for it and they wanted predictability.”
While the advisors—academic clinicians from various institutions—urged the foundation to conduct an in-person natural history study, the organization stuck with the medical records approach and the trial was accepted into the RDEP program.
Fitter cautioned, however, that as the gene therapy is still investigational, “it is yet to be seen whether our control of medical records will be accepted at the BLA.”
Innovative trial designs are one area where Davis believes artificial intelligence holds “a lot of promise,” particularly when it comes to analyzing volumes of natural history or real-world data that are inherently less controlled than results from a clinical trial.
AI can also play a role in accelerating biomarker and endpoint development, Davis added. “With tens of thousands of rare diseases, with most of them with no treatments, there’s going to be a lot of work for biomarkers and . . . a lot of them will be very specific to the condition being studied.”
Data sharing is another key focus for the agency. This is particularly true when it comes to natural history studies, Amy Comstock Rick, associate director for Rare Disease Strategy and director of Strategic Coalitions for FDA’s Rare Disease Innovation Hub, told BioSpace at BIO. There is a need for “more natural history studies that are in a place where people can access them” to inform rare disease drug development programs more broadly.
The FDA’s new rare disease framework appears to support this approach, as it highlights “building shared resources, robust training, and institutional knowledge on rare disease drug development and review” as a primary focus.
The challenges ahead
The experts who spoke with BioSpace all acknowledged that many challenges remain when it comes to bringing effective therapies to the 1 in 10 Americans currently living with a rare disease. One obstacle the new framework aims to address is the regulatory unpredictability that has recently plagued the space .
“The more predictable the framework is, I think that will help make investors and companies feel more comfortable investing in it because they won’t be thinking about the sort of unpredictability of flexibility exercised at the end, when the program is done,” Davis said.
This is particularly true in the ultrarare disease space, Davis added, where finding partners to support drug development can be difficult.
Fitter spoke to this issue in her statement provided at last month’s public meeting, requesting that the FDA’s guidance also be written for patient groups going it alone.
She asked the agency to “write this guidance for patient advocacy groups as sponsors, not only drug companies. The FOXG1 Research Foundation sponsors our trial. There is no pharma partner. In ultra-rare disease, more programs will look like ours, because no one else is coming. Build the framework for us too.”
Government

The FDA’s drug review process can often be “unpredictable,” and review teams typically “differ greatly” in what they ask of drug sponsors, Sen. Bill Cassidy said.

General Motors said they can't, and they won't build a manual C8 Chevrolet Corvette. Well, Peitz Performance did it. They entirely reengineered the car to make room for a manual six-speed transaxle and invited the Shelby American president to do donuts in it.
The last time the Chevrolet Corvette lineup featured a factory manual transmission was the 2019 model year, which marked the end of the seventh-generation C7 production. The final Corvette with a gear shifter was a black 2019 Z06 coupe , featuring a seven-speed manual that rolled off the production line of the Bowling Green Assembly Plant in Kentucky on November 14, 2019. The model was later auctioned off for charity for $2.7 million.
When the mid-engine eighth generation launched for the 2020 model year, Chevrolet eliminated the manual option entirely due to structural design constraints and low consumer demand, which had dropped by roughly 22% by 2019. The current lineup relies exclusively on the Tremec dual-clutch automatic transmission.
Furthermore, earlier this year, C8 Corvette executive chief engineer Tony Roma shut down rumors about a potential manual transmission when rumors started making the rounds after Tremec displayed a manual transmission at SEMA in late 2025.
Photo: Alex Peitz | YouTube While General Motors went on the "no can do" strategy, Peitz Performance came out saying, "Oh, yes, we can!" Because the C8 Corvette is engineered around the eight-speed dual-clutch automatic transmission, building a true manual required re-engineering the car.
Peitz Performance used a Tremec-built, brand-new TR-9060 six-speed manual transaxle, designed to handle up to 1,000 pound-feet of torque and adapt the differential right from the C8’s stock dual-clutch housing.
The transmission is operated with the help of a custom cable-driven shifter , heavily modified from a Porsche aftermarket setup. To give the driver a third pedal, Peitz integrated a modified clutch assembly, taken straight from a Cadillac CT4-V Blackwing.
The biggest hurdle was the car’s computer. The Peitz engineers managed to bypass GM’s locked factory setup, using a high-end MoTeC M182 plug-and-play ECU, paired with an M150 TCU. The setup allows the car to run flawlessly without dashboard error codes, while enabling downshift throttle blips and automatic upshift ignition cuts.
Photo: Alex Peitz | YouTube To prove what the manual Corvette can do, Peitz Performance invited the President of Shelby American to see what it can do. Gary Patterson crossed the enemy lines, took the manual 'Vette for a spin and did donuts in it.
Peitz Performance lists the complete turn-key conversion package at a staggering $74,528.999. The specialized MoTeC electronics alone drive a huge portion of that price. But as the company is still working on the electronics, customer availability is slated for July 2027.
You must provide the C8 Corvette yourself. This means that a Corvette Stingray with a row-your-own gearbox is roughly $148,000. In the meantime, manual-swapping a brand-new Corvette ZR1X would push the cost into extreme hypercar territory, putting your total expected investment at roughly $302,000.

MG Motor Treats Australia to a Special Edition of the Successful MG4 EV Urban All-Electric Hatchback
28 photos
Photo: MG Motor Australia
MG Motor Australia is giving its popular MG4 EV Urban a fresh makeover with the MG4 EV Urban Special Edition, priced at AU $33,990, including a $2,000 cashback offer on the drive-away price. That’s just a little more than $23k, which isn't bad at all.
MG was established in England in 1924, and more than a century later Morris Garages has gained a new lease of life thanks to the Chinese automotive manufacturer SAIC Motor. Currently, “MG offers a broad range of vehicles to suit all needs, including battery electric , advanced hybrid, petrol and diesel, making the latest automotive technologies more accessible than ever.” To support its affordability claims, here’s the latest version of one of their accessible EV models, ready for primetime in Australia.
MG Motor launched the MG4 EV, or MG4 Electric, as an all-electric small family car (C-segment) in the summer of 2022 at home in China. It quickly traveled that year to the Old Continent and other markets, helping “make EV ownership more affordable, practical and enjoyable for everyday drivers,” according to the company. Last year, MG launched a second version, called MG4 EV Urban, based on the newer SAIC E3 electric vehicle architecture using a cell-to-body battery design and featuring FWD only.
Now, MG Motor Australia is refreshing the MG4 EV Urban with a limited-edition model, “bringing exclusive styling enhancements and added interior ambience to one of Australia’s most accessible electric vehicles.” It comes with exclusive features like a contrasting, black-painted roof, black exterior mirrors, ambient lighting integrated into the door panels, and an all-new Ice Blue metallic exterior paint color, among other things.
The special edition will have Ice Blue and the existing Diamond Red as the exclusive two-color offerings. It’s available now for purchase through MG dealerships nationwide, and the Special Edition costs AU $1k more than the entry-level MG4 EV Urban Essence 54. The Special Edition retains the Essence 54 specification and comes with the larger 54kWh battery configuration, enough for a range of up to 405 km (WLTP) or 252 miles.
It also has DC fast charging from 10 to 80 percent in approximately 30 minutes, seating for five, 382 liters (13.49 cu-ft) for the luggage compartment and an additional 98 liters (3.46 cu-ft) under the boot, Front Wheel Drive, as well as a five-star ANCAP safety rating. All MG4 EV Urban models have a 10-year warranty when serviced within MG’s national dealer network.
“The MG4 EV Urban has proven to be a popular choice with Australian buyers, and we think this Special Edition will build on that appeal. It’s already a great car, so we’ve added a few distinctive touches to make it even more appealing. The Special Edition will be limited to just 750 units in Australia, and we’re excited to see customers get behind it,” said Dimitri Andreatidis, Marketing Director at MG Motor Australia.

Europe, Be Prepared! Stellantis Is Launching the Ram Rampage With Two Versions and Two Powertrains
11 photos
Photo: Ram Trucks
Stellantis is eager to capitalize on Ram Trucks' relaunch everywhere, and the Old Continent is getting its own version of the ultra-popular Ram Rampage , which has been wreaking havoc across Latin America, as far as customer hearts are concerned.
At home in North America, Stellantis has pulled a rabbit out of the proverbial hat with the Ram Trucks’ return to Hemi V8 form, and the brand quickly reaped the benefits and climbed to the number one spot among the company’s brands in the United States sales charts, besting Jeep in the process. As prices continue to rise and put pressure on people, mid-size trucks are the next holy grail – and Ram will soon join the likes of Toyota and GM alongside newcomers like Hyundai.
But over in Europe, where there aren’t any vast expanses like in North America, even mid-size pickup trucks might be too large and unwieldy, so the company has found a quick solution to the predicament: Stellantis previewed the potential of the Latin America-born Ram Rampage at the Fieracavalli 2025 event, with the 127th edition of the equestrian-dedicated outing featuring the European introduction of the Rampage.
Now, a year later from the Veronafiere exhibition center premiere in Verona, Italy, the American brand announced that Ram Rampage orders are now open on the Old Continent, with the new model being positioned “between traditional pickups and high-end SUVs” as a lifestyle choice: it “combines the versatility of a genuine pickup with the refinement, technology and ease of use expected from an SUV.”
Dubbed as a Premium Compact Lifestyle Pickup, Rampage will have two distinct versions, each featuring a dedicated powertrain: Rebel 2.2 Turbodiesel and R/T 2.0 Turbo Petrol. The Ram Rampage may be considered a compact truck in North America, but in Europe it’s very close to a mid-range offering: it’s 5,028 mm (197.95 inches) long and 1,886 mm (74.25 in.) wide.
Alas, unlike traditional pickup trucks, it features a unibody architecture, independent suspension and a multilink rear layout. It does come with an on-demand 4x4 system featuring 4WD Low and Hill Descent Control settings, plus a 1,450 mm-long (57 inches) cargo bed, suitable for a Euro pallet, with payload capacity of up to 1,015 kg (2,238 pounds), depending on the version.
“Rampage brings a bold new expression of RAM to Europe: unmistakable strength and capability, premium comfort and effortless everyday usability. Its European-friendly dimensions deliver true pickup versatility—without compromise,” says Fabio Catone, Head of Ram & Dodge Brands, Enlarged Europe.
The Ram Rampage Rebel is dedicated to more utilitarian tasks, with the 2.2L Turbodiesel engine packing 200 ponies and 450 Nm or 332 lb-ft of torque. It features 17-inch wheels and all-terrain tires, and “the result is a lifestyle pickup designed to move naturally between work and urban environments, particularly adapted to European roads.”
Meanwhile, the Ram Rampage R/T is the performance-focused version with the 2.0-liter Turbo Petrol engine packing 272 horsepower and 400 Nm or 295 lb-ft of torque, 19-inch alloy wheels, a 10-mm lowered suspension, and a tuned sport exhaust. It’s capable of reaching 100 kph or 62 mph in just 6.9 seconds and a top speed of 220 kph or 137 mph. But it’s also less potent when hauling – the payload capacity drops to 750 kg or 1,653 pounds, though it retains the 4x4 setup, at least.
Pricing kicks off from a 'suggested' €44 sans taxes, and first deliveries are scheduled for February 2027.So, what do you think?

2028 Mazda CX-5 MPS Is a CGI Turbo Hybrid SUV That Seeks the Return of the Mazda Performance Series
17 photos
Photo: AutoYa Interior / YouTube
There has been a lot of commotion early this month across the automotive world, as the mid-fall event season has featured a double ensemble – EICMA in Italy for two-wheeled fans and the SEMA Show in Las Vegas for the four-wheel aficionados with a knack for aftermarket builds.
Mazda, because it suits our discussion, was only present – unofficially – at one of them, with a YouTuber aiming to shut down Nevada with the “ ultimate SEMA machine ,” an older Mazda MX-5 Miata featuring a 960 cubic-inch (15.73-liter) 13-rotor quat-turbo engine: this enthusiast stacked a triple-turbo 12-rotor motor onto a regular single-rotor turbo engine and reached seven feet in height with it!
Of course, there were other, less outrageous things happening with Mazda. Such as MNAO ( Mazda North America Operations ) nailing a great month across the US automotive market. Indeed, MNAO reported total October sales of 31,446 vehicles, an increase of 25 percent compared to last year and its second-best October deliveries.
Year-to-date sales have reached 341,714 vehicles, which is almost one percent down from last year after weak initial sales during the first part of the year. So, how do they increase customer engagement and continue on the path of recovery?
Officially, Mazda has kicked off the season to be jolly early in November by launching its annual Winter Sales Event, which features “attractive customer cash savings and special APR financing rates for qualified buyers on certain 2026 model year vehicles” until January 4, 2027. But do you know exactly what could be more attractive than that?
Well, according to the rumor mill and their helper from across the parallel universes of vehicular CGI (a member of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators), maybe a 2027 Mazda CX-5 MPS featuring the return of the Mazda Performance Series could become a ton more amazing for customers.
At the moment, it’s only done in CGI, though, as the good folks over at the " AutoYa " info channel on YouTube have a satellite venue dubbed " AutoYa Interior, " which is where all the CGI Mazda action resides. The host of the channel muses that the all-new, third-generation Mazda CX-5 compact crossover SUV has already reached the dealerships across all global markets, including in the United States.
However, there’s only the gasoline powertrain option, and everyone is waiting for Mazda to launch the all-new in-house-developed hybrid setup. But what if, to celebrate its release and also compete with the powerful Toyota RAV4 GR Sport, Mazda would also reveal a sports-oriented version with a turbocharged hybrid or even a plug-in hybrid powertrain featuring the return of the MPS - Mazda Performance Series nameplate?
Well, they went on and created it for us in their latest unofficial, hypothetical design project with the help of their resident virtual artist – the 2027 or 2028 Mazda CX-5 MPS, showcased both inside and outside, complete with a host of ritzy color options. Cool or not?

Ducati Gives Away a $270 Meccano Monster Set, But There's a Catch
10 photos
Photo: Meccano
As the EICMA motorcycle show was unfolding over in Milan, Italy, last week, local bike maker Ducati didn't really focus on impressing the crowds there. For one reason or another, the company didn't really bring anything worth drooling over to the event, despite the presence there of three new SP motorcycles and the 2027 Panigale V4, among others.
Ducati's UK arm, though, did something this particular company doesn't do very often: it announced an online competition that will end with one lucky guy or girl getting their hands on a toy model motorcycle many go nuts over: a Meccano interpretation of the Monster.
The British toy maker tied the knot once again with Ducati to produce toy replicas of Italian motorcycles in the spring of this year, and to mark the occasion, it rolled out the so-called Meccano Pro Ducati Monster construction set.
Comprising 315 real metal parts, the set can be assembled using the two included tools to form one of the wildest interpretations of the naked motorcycle, basically a metal skeleton that looks as wild and aggressive as the real thing.
Coming in at a scale of 1:12 when complete, the finished set includes multi-piece wheels, working steering, and even a coil-spring suspension system. Finishing everything off is a set of stickers meant to give the model the proper Ducati look, but also a display stand to show off the build.
For the purpose of the online competition, Meccano is not offering the set alone, but accompanied by a large red hoodie, a shield sign, a black cap, and an art mug - everything a 16-year-old or older fan of these two brands would need so close to Christmas, and something which would normally cost some £200 ($268 at today's exchange rates).
To get a chance to win the set, there is a catch: you must be a UK resident only, and you need to follow Meccano and Ducati UK on Instagram . Once you've done that, you must like the post announcing the giveaway, and comment with the phrase "Built to Win." The online competition ends on November 18, so not much time is left.
As for the Monster, the family of naked bikes did make the news ahead of the EICMA show, as Ducati presented at the beginning of the month an all-black back-to-basics version meant for purists.
The bike is not mechanically different from the current fifth generation, but comes with a total black livery, unpainted exhaust end caps and snorkel, and a bison-back fuel tank – all of them as a means to make the Dark look like the original Monster from the early 1990s.
Ducati will launch the Monster Dark onto the market at the end of this month, and it is asking £10,995, including VAT ($14,700).

source_document.body:
SK pharmteco’s Tatiana Nanda, chief technical officer of SK pharmteco Viral Vector North America discusses what gene therapy sponsors must account for sooner rather than later when preparing for GMP manufacturing.
Preclinical manufacturing isn’t simply about generating material. Done well, it generates the data and process understanding needed to make better development decisions.
By the time a gene therapy program reaches Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) manufacturing, opportunities to address issues identified during earlier development can become more limited, costly and time-consuming.
SK pharmteco’s Tatiana Nanda, chief technical officer of Viral Vector North America, spoke to BioSpace about how sponsors can set themselves up for success before they reach the GMP manufacturing stage so they can avoid costly delays and dose shortages.
1. Three Key CMC goals
Many gene therapy programs focus on getting material into preclinical studies as quickly as possible. However, at initiation, program developers should consider the purpose of their preclinical campaigns, according to Nanda. From a chemistry, manufacturing and controls (CMC) perspective, she said, there are ultimately three goals:
Answer scientific questions about scalability and manufacturability. This allows sponsors to determine whether an early research process can be developed into one suitable for GMP manufacturing.
Generate the large volumes of material needed before GMP. Very often, companies underestimate the amount required for nonhuman primate studies, stability tests, analytical and drug product development.
Derisk GMP, especially as GMP manufacturing is very expensive in terms of time and finances. Small-scale studies often mask issues that appear at full scale, such as longer hold times, higher impurity loads and modality‑specific sensitivities.
Nanda also noted that pilot-scale runs help determine whether a process is truly GMP‑ready and prevent costly surprises once in the GMP suite.
2. Preclinical or pilot-scale manufacturing insights
A well-designed preclinical or pilot-scale manufacturing campaign can help ensure that sponsors have critical information before entering GMP manufacturing. Pilot campaigns, for example, can uncover the operator‑dependent steps that are often underestimated, according to Nanda.
Depending on the program’s maturity and objectives, early development-scale studies or pilot-scale manufacturing campaigns can provide different levels of process understanding, helping sponsors determine where further optimization is needed before GMP.
“We have a very good understanding of platforms,” she said. “However, depending on the specific modality, and in the case of AAV-specific serotypes, you may be able to identify operator-dependent steps early on in your preclinical campaign.”
In addition, Nanda noted, a preclinical campaign allows a sponsor to educate GMP operators early on and provide training on how to identify and mitigate errors and recover any losses across different unit operations.
“Frequently, a week or two of additional optimization work will result in significantly better yields,” she said. Plus, well-designed pilot-scale campaigns, in addition to resolving yield issues, provide early insight into cost of goods sold, dose availability and the number of GMP batches required, according to Nanda. She also noted that full-scale pilot runs validate assumptions, such as whether one batch can support an entire Phase 1 trial, and help prevent situations in which a sponsor plans to dose 20 patients but ultimately has sufficient material for only 10.
Tatiana Nanda, chief technical officer of SK pharmteco Viral Vector North America
3. Analytical testing and process characterization
Analytical testing and process characterization can influence development strategy beyond generating release data. Analytics, for example, guide development decisions, according to Nanda.
“Having robust analytics actually tells you whether you’re on the right path or not,” she said. Nanda added that fit‑for‑purpose assays with proper sensitivity and accuracy help sponsors identify impurities, quantify them and ensure that potency assays measure attributes that meaningfully inform dose and product performance.
While the field is still learning how to interpret gene therapy analytics, according to Nanda, collecting robust data early and throughout the preclinical campaign is essential for connecting process, quality, safety and dose metrics. She recommended drafting a critical quality attribute document early to define what matters and build a set of assays around those factors. In turn, those assays can allow a sponsor to devise the analytical strategy.
4. Early process knowledge capture
Capturing process knowledge early can make technology transfer, GMP execution and future regulatory interactions more successful. As Nanda explained, sponsors must document decision rationale, not just the steps taken. She noted that this is important because as the CMC life cycle extends from early development to late-phase and commercial manufacturing, regulators may ask about the rationale behind parameter selection and process changes. Technology transfers may occur at multiple points in a product’s life cycle.
Consequently, having documentation properly formulated, stored and connected as the product moves through the CMC cycle supports regulatory submissions and future commercial manufacturing campaigns, Nanda said.
5. Finding the right CDMO
When selecting a viral vector contract development and manufacturing organization (CDMO), it’s important to know what separates a CDMO that simply manufactures batches from one that actively helps sponsors reduce technical and development risk.
A strong CDMO serves as an extension of the sponsor’s CMC capabilities by challenging assumptions, prioritizing development work, advising how and where to invest in process development and integrating analytical and manufacturing teams, according to Nanda. Cross‑trained teams, not only in GMP and quality control, but also process and analytical, manufacturing science and technology, and regulatory expectations can address challenges, she said.
In addition, she noted that CDMOs with commercial experience provide early insight into future challenges and help avoid expensive late‑phase tech transfers.
6. Mistakes sponsors make
Before entering GMP manufacturing, sponsors tend to make a few common mistakes. For example, Nanda said, they often underestimate analytical development and understanding their drug product.
Too often, the focus is on the amount of drug substance to be made rather than understanding formulation, stability and product handling, she explained. Nanda said this is particularly important when it comes to particularly sensitive modalities such as lentiviral vectors, where storage, thawing, preparation and administration can all affect product performance.
Downstream yield and purity are also overlooked, according to Nanda. When it comes to short-term innovation in the gene therapy space, she said, downstream recovery is a major opportunity, as upstream scale is irrelevant if downstream recovery is only 10%.
The path forward
For sponsors preparing for IND/IMPD-enabling studies, the message is clear: the path to GMP manufacturing begins well before the GMP batch. Early process development, analytical strategy, pilot-scale manufacturing and careful knowledge capture can help sponsors understand whether their process is scalable, their assays are informative and their material strategy can support the next stage of development. By addressing these areas earlier, gene therapy developers can move toward GMP manufacturing with greater confidence and fewer avoidable surprises.

Stellantis Gets Ready to Go Green With Marvel Studios' Avengers: Doomsday Universe Collab With Jeep
7 photos
Photo: Stellantis
Stellantis is expertly tapping into every possible channel to secure its return back to form in America, with special emphasis on the Jeep brand, which has received special attention as of lately.
We have seen things like the new series of Direct Connection Hemi V8 crate engines, but there was also the SRT Performance with the first-ever Jeep Wrangler Scrambler concept, and the brand also happily announced what’s new for a multitude of its 2027 model year vehicles. But there was also the new brand strategy for Jeep announced at the 2026 Paris Motor Show for Europe and the conclusion of the bold Twelve 4 Twelve series with the 2027 Jeep Wrangler Switchback as the grand finale.
Well, no worries, as there is more Jeep news coming: “one universe was never going to be enough for the Jeep brand.” As such, the marque and Marvel have teamed up for a yearlong collaboration, and to bring it to a conclusion ahead of the Marvel Studios’ Avengers: Doomsday movie, they launched “A Jeep 4x4 for Any Universe,” a new co-branded marketing campaign launching in the United States and select global markets.
It is coming to life as a setup toward the theatrical release of Marvel Studios’ Avengers: Doomsday, which arrives on December 18. It’s a 360-degree marketing campaign that will include national and dealership support across broadcast, social media, website, CRM, and experiential events, with both US and global events. For the yearlong campaign’s conclusion, the Jeep brand jumps into the worlds of Avengers: Doomsday, featuring in the home universes of the Avengers, Fantastic Four, and X-Men.
The “multiversal creative journey” includes legendary Marvel characters, including Captain America, the Human Torch, H.E.R.B.I.E., and Nightcrawler. The campaign also has a “signature moment” where The Thing gets behind the wheel of a Jeep Wrangler, “bringing together one of Marvel’s most formidable heroes and the Jeep brand’s most iconic 4x4.”
The collaboration originally started in May with “Origin Story,” which introduced the 2026 Jeep Wrangler America250 special edition, which features an exclusive Captain America shield tire cover. There was even an original, limited-edition Marvel comic book cover featuring Captain America and the Jeep Wrangler America250.
“The Original Superheroes” continued the story over the summer with a switch from comic book superheroes to real-life US military veterans: the Jeep Wrangler, Grand Cherokee, Cherokee, Gladiator, Grand Wagoneer, and Compass vehicles were driven by veterans. As a note, both the Avengers: Doomsday blockbuster from Marvel Studios and Dune: Part Three from Warner Bros. Pictures are releasing on the same day, earning them both the ‘Dunesday’ nickname.
It happened before with ‘Barbenheimer,’ a viral pop-culture phenomenon surrounding the simultaneous theatrical release of Barbie and Oppenheimer during the summer of 2023. Now it’s a race to see if Dunesday performs even better, as the previous event was a rare moment of crowd-going cinema during the age of streaming.
